title: Nvidia’s China Partners and the PLA - The Wire China
gist: A procurement-records investigation finds that at least 23 of Nvidia's ~123 listed Chinese partners have since 2022 won bids to supply Entity-Listed or PLA-affiliated buyers, including five of the Seven Sons of National Defense universities, subsidiaries of three major defense contractors and a PLA unit under the Academy of Military Sciences. The reporting maps how Entity-Listed firms such as Sugon, Hygon and Inspur appear to be reconstituted through newly registered partner companies, how Chinese state entities own stakes above 10 percent in at least 17 Nvidia partners, and why military-civil fusion makes end-use verification through the reseller channel structurally unreliable.

themes.theme: Partner-channel leakage to the Chinese defense base

insights.claim: At least 23 of the roughly 123 Chinese companies Nvidia lists as partners have won bids since 2022 to supply universities, companies and labs that the U.S. placed on the Entity List for military ties — roughly a fifth of Nvidia's China partner base.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Headline compliance with export controls does not cover the indirect reseller channel — a live regulatory and headline risk for NVDA that Washington can act on without any new legislation.
insights.quote: Since 2022 at least 23 Chinese companies that Nvidia names as partners have won bids to supply universities, companies and labs that the U.S. has added to the Entity List for their ties to China’s military, according to a review of procurement records.
insights.locator: Since 2022 at least 23 Chinese companies

insights.claim: The buyers awarding contracts to Nvidia partners include five of the seven 'Seven Sons of National Defense' universities, subsidiaries of three of China's largest defense contractors, and a unit of the People's Liberation Army itself.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: The end-customer list is exactly the population U.S. controls were designed to exclude, strengthening the case for tightening rules on non-controlled hardware.
insights.quote: These include five of the seven schools known as “China’s Seven Sons of National Defense”; subsidiaries of three of China’s largest defense contractors; and a unit of the People’s Liberation Army itself.
insights.locator: These include five of the seven schools

insights.claim: The average contract awarded to an Nvidia partner by an Entity List or military-affiliated Chinese entity was worth only about 1.7 million yuan (roughly $250,000), meaning the leakage occurs through a high volume of small, low-visibility transactions rather than headline deals.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Small ticket sizes make this flow nearly invisible in revenue disclosures and hard to police — expect enforcement to target the channel structure, not individual deals.
insights.quote: The average contract awarded to an Nvidia partner by an Entity List or military-affiliated entity was worth around 1.7 million yuan (~$250,000).

insights.claim: Some Chinese military-linked tenders explicitly solicited Nvidia chips or hardware matching Nvidia specifications, even though procurement records do not confirm that Nvidia products were actually delivered in every deal.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Demand-side intent is documented in Chinese procurement language itself — the strongest available evidence that Nvidia silicon remains the preferred input for Chinese defense-linked compute.
insights.quote: though some tenders explicitly solicited Nvidia chips or those that matched Nvidia specifications
insights.locator: The records did not show that each of the deals

insights.claim: Nvidia's public defense is that membership in its partner network confers no product access and that China already has millions of domestic chips, more than enough for every military use.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Nvidia is publicly arguing that controls are futile because domestic substitutes suffice — the same argument it uses to lobby for looser China rules.
insights.quote: The U.S. government has strictly controlled sales to China since 2022, and today China has millions of domestic chips, more than enough for every military use.
insights.locator: Companies are always free to join Nvidia’s ‘partner network’

insights.claim: Nvidia declined to answer questions about the due diligence it performs on its Chinese partners or whether it knew that around a fifth of them had sought to supply Entity List or PLA-affiliated buyers.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Non-response on vetting is the disclosure gap Congress and Commerce will probe next; treat partner-network governance as an unquantified NVDA liability.
insights.locator: Nvidia did not respond to questions about the due diligence

insights.claim: Former State Department China technology adviser Ryan Fedasiuk argues American technology companies doing business in China bear an affirmative duty to know where their products end up and to prevent military or intelligence end use.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Signals the policy direction: shifting the compliance burden from government licensing onto vendor know-your-customer obligations.
insights.quote: It is incumbent on American companies doing business in China, especially technology companies, to make sure that they know where their products are going and that they aren’t being misused for military or intelligence end uses.
insights.locator: “Nvidia should be doing more due diligence,”

themes.theme: Where the export-control line currently sits

insights.claim: Biden-era export controls have blocked Nvidia's most advanced chips from China since 2022, but the Trump administration has loosened them to allow H200 sales to licensed Chinese customers while Blackwell chips remain controlled.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: The tradeable boundary is now H200 legal / Blackwell blocked — any move of Blackwell across that line is the next major China-revenue catalyst for NVDA.
insights.quote: The U.S. now allows Nvidia to sell its H200 chip, which had been export controlled since 2023, to licensed customers in China. Nvidia’s more advanced Blackwell chips remain controlled.
insights.locator: Export controls imposed by the Biden administration

insights.claim: Beijing has blocked its own companies from importing H200s, yet Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler testified on July 14 that a small number of H200 sales into China have still gone through.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: The binding constraint on Nvidia's China H200 revenue is currently Chinese import policy, not U.S. licensing — a demand block Washington cannot fix.
insights.locator: While Beijing has blocked its companies from importing H200s

insights.claim: U.S. export controls have never applied to Nvidia's lower-end hardware, which the company distributes through its partner network and which some Chinese partners integrate into their own products.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: The uncontrolled low-end plus reseller integration is the structural gap; closing it would hit a revenue line nobody currently models as at risk.
insights.quote: The controls have never applied to Nvidia’s lower-end hardware, which the company distributes through a network of partners.
insights.locator: The controls have never applied

insights.claim: Anything made in or shipped from the United States to an Entity List buyer requires a license that is met with a presumption of denial, regardless of how mundane the item is.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Explains why the leakage runs through non-U.S.-origin, below-threshold hardware sold by Chinese intermediaries rather than direct exports.
insights.quote: If it was made in or shipped from the U.S. — if it’s a toothbrush or server — license required, license denied,
insights.locator: Companies cannot export goods from the U.S.

insights.claim: Chinese firms can legally sell Nvidia products to Entity-Listed universities provided the goods are made outside the U.S., fall below technological thresholds and contain limited controlled inputs, and Georgetown's CSET estimated in 2023 that at least 27 Nvidia products require no license for sale in China.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A legal, licence-free product surface of at least 27 SKUs exists — control tightening would have to attack the threshold definitions themselves.
insights.quote: In 2023, analysts at Georgetown’s CSET estimated that at least 27 Nvidia products do not require a license for sale in China.
insights.locator: Companies in China can legally sell some Nvidia products

insights.claim: Scrutiny of Nvidia's channel intensified after the co-founder of Supermicro — one of Nvidia's U.S. partners — was indicted and charged with chip smuggling.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Criminal exposure has already reached a U.S.-listed Nvidia partner; partner-network risk is not purely a Chinese-entity issue.
insights.locator: As the company’s activities in China attract growing scrutiny

themes.theme: Entity-Listed firms reconstituted as new partners

insights.claim: Changkuai Computing, an Nvidia partner claiming a 2023 founding, uses an internet content provider number registered to Entity-Listed chipmaker Hygon, files patents naming the same three inventors as Sugon and Nettrix, and markets its servers in almost identical language to Nettrix.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Entity listings appear to be routed around by spinning up fresh corporate wrappers — designation-based controls decay within months unless re-audited.
insights.locator: Another relatively new Nvidia partner, Changkuai

insights.claim: The U.S. added Hygon and its top shareholder Sugon to the Entity List in 2019 and later accused Sugon of building supercomputers for the PLA, then added Nettrix — founded in 2019 by former Sugon executives — to the Entity List in 2025 for providing significant manufacturing capabilities to Sugon.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A six-year documented pattern of one designated supercomputing cluster regenerating under new names — the base rate for successor-entity evasion is high.
insights.locator: The U.S. added Hygon and its top shareholder, Sugon

insights.claim: Nvidia partner Rithmax (Xiamen Yuanchou) shares registered phone numbers with Inspur subsidiaries, markets four servers using Inspur's own product language, and has at least 22 patent inventors whose names match those on patents from another Inspur subsidiary.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Inspur, delisted from Nvidia's partner page after its 2023 Entity listing, appears to persist inside the channel through a differently named partner.
insights.locator: In business registration paperwork filed with Chinese regulators

insights.claim: Nvidia and Inspur partnered as early as 2009 and Nvidia executives publicly called Inspur one of its most strategic server partners globally, before the U.S. accused Inspur of supporting Chinese military modernization and Entity-Listed it in 2023.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Nvidia's most strategic Chinese server partner became a sanctioned entity within four years — a template for how quickly a China channel relationship can be revalued to zero.

insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Third-country transshipment through Singapore remains an active investigative thread that can trigger further designations.

insights.claim: Roughly a third of Nvidia's Chinese partners were founded in the past decade, and the youngest — Apex AI Computing (Beijing), an AI server provider whose largest indirect shareholder is listed cloud firm Teamsun — was registered only in February of this year.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A young, fast-churning partner roster is inherently hard to vet — corporate age is a usable red-flag screen for channel risk.

themes.theme: State ownership inside the Nvidia channel

insights.claim: Chinese government entities hold stakes of more than 10 percent in at least 17 of Nvidia's Chinese partners, including ZTE, xFusion (41 percent China Mobile), China Greatwall Technology (40.6 percent China Electronics Corporation) and Tsinghua Tongfang (34.1 percent China National Nuclear Corporation).
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A material slice of Nvidia's China distribution is owned by entities on the Treasury Chinese Military-Industrial Complex list — an easy target for the next sanctions tranche.
insights.quote: Chinese government entities hold stakes of more than 10 percent in at least 17 of Nvidia’s partners in China, according to corporate records collated by WireScreen.
insights.locator: Chinese government entities hold stakes

insights.claim: Maginfra, a firm owned by a Jinan government asset manager and registered only in February 2025, signed a 1.1 billion yuan ($162 million) deal in November to supply IT equipment to a listed arm of the China Development Bank and has reportedly won a licence to buy H200s alongside a ZTE unit.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A one-year-old state-owned vehicle is already writing $162m compute contracts and holding H200 import licences — watch it as a proxy for how China channels licensed U.S. silicon.
insights.locator: Maginfra is a newly created firm that was registered in February 2025

insights.claim: Maginfra lists an address in the same Jinan office complex as an Inspur subsidiary, and a third Nvidia partner, Xiamen Yuanchou, registered an office in that complex last April.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Shared-address clustering is a cheap, replicable screen for identifying successor entities to sanctioned Chinese hardware firms.

insights.claim: SinoInfo, a Beijing reseller that calls itself an Nvidia 'elite partner' and posts an approval letter from Nvidia executive John Leggio to sell data center products in mainland China, simultaneously lists Chinese missile makers CASIC and CASC among its own partners.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Defense affiliations are advertised publicly on partner websites, meaning basic open-source vetting would have surfaced them — a hard fact pattern for Nvidia to defend.

insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A 13-person firm sitting in Nvidia's official partner directory transacting directly with a PLA research unit is the single most quotable fact for policymakers pushing channel restrictions.

insights.so_what: End-use certification as a compliance tool is structurally unreliable in China, which pushes policy toward blanket entity- or capability-based bans.
